molasses.title: Molasse and its weathering
description: The cathedral of Lausanne was built with a local molasse sandstone, that is particularly sensitive to water.
You may obtain directly here information on that stone as well as on its weathering by clicking on the corresponding buttons
You may also go directly to an interactive discovery App to use as you walk around the cathedral.
The Lausanne Cathedral is built from a variety of stones originating from different quarries all around Switzerland and some parts of Germany.

During the 19th century, the regional molasse sandstone of exposed architectural elements of the Cathedral was replaced with limestones and “harder” sandstones from the wider region of the canton Vaud.
In the 20th century, due to the scarcity of regional quarries, the general substitution of local molasse sandstone for maintenance and restoration became common practice.
A variety of replacement sandstones from Fribourg, Bern, Zug, and Hannover (Oberkirchen, Germany) were utilized in its place.
It is a molassic sandstone from Lausanne and was placed in the Cathedral in the 12th Century CE (Gothic period).
It is a type of sedimentary stone which is predominant on the south tower of the Transept. This sandstone most likely came from the nearby quarries.
This stone is particularly sensitive to water due to the presence of swelling clays.
As part of this formation, the “Molasse grise de Lausanne” was extracted right outside the medieval city center and employed to erect the Lausanne Cathedral.

Over the centuries, sandstones of the same typology were brought in from different local quarries distributed around the medieval centre and employed for modification and maintenance works at the Cathedral.
